one_liner: Rust zero-copy serialization crate; faster serialize and in-place reads than Rust FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto, prost and rmp-serde.
what_it_does: rkyv writes Rust values into a byte buffer laid out as an 'archived' twin of each type (#[repr(C)] structs, fixed-endian primitives, relative pointers). A reader casts the buffer to &ArchivedT and uses it directly, with no parse step. You derive Archive/Serialize/Deserialize on ordinary Rust types; there is no IDL or codegen step. The API is rkyv::to_bytes, then either rkyv::access (validated) or unsafe access_unchecked, plus deserialize/from_bytes when you need the native type back; it is not wire-compatible with any baseline.
how_it_is_fast: Total zero-copy deserialization: the archived bytes are the in-memory representation, and internal references are relative pointers (RelPtr, a 32-bit offset from the pointer's own address by default). Access is therefore a pointer offset plus a cast (1.09 ns on every dataset), and it works on read-only memory-mapped buffers. Serialization is a single write-forward pass that places leaves first and the root last, using per-type resolvers and a reusable scratch arena instead of per-object heap allocations. Collections are archived as ready-to-query structures: a SwissTable hash map (SSE2/NEON group probing, target-independent FxHash) and a B-tree. The optional bytecheck validation is a separate upfront pass that checks bounds and subtree ranges without allocating.
when_to_use: Both writer and reader are Rust and you load large read-mostly data (game assets, caches, precomputed indexes, memory-mapped files) where parse time dominates: access is constant-time and reads run in place (log dataset unvalidated read 8.33 µs vs 42.2 µs for Rust FlatBuffers).
You want to query archived HashMap/BTreeMap/Rc-shared data in place without rebuilding it; rkyv archives these natively, which Cap'n Proto and FlatBuffers do not.
Serialize-heavy Rust pipelines now using prost, rmp-serde, capnp or flatbuffers: 2.7x to 7.4x faster serialize on the log dataset, and faster on all four datasets.

Untrusted input that must still be checked: validated access on log costs 274 µs vs 2.14 ms for FlatBuffers validated. For data you trust (checksummed or signed, or your own files), unsafe access_unchecked removes that cost entirely.
no_std or no-alloc targets: the std and alloc features can be turned off, and CI cross-builds thumbv6m-none-eabi.
when_not_to_use: Any non-Rust producer or consumer, C++ included: there is no C API, and the project's own feature matrix lists cross-language support as 'no'.

You need schema evolution or forward/backward compatibility: the feature matrix says no. Archives stay readable only if the Rust type, the format-control features and a semver-compatible rkyv version are all unchanged. Versioning is manual, for example the AsBox wrapper trick in examples/backwards_compat.rs.

Wire size or bandwidth is the bottleneck: the log buffer is 1,011,488 B, against 703,710 B for bitcode, 784,997 B for rmp-serde and 884,628 B for prost. Unset fields, padding and pointers all take space.

You only need the fastest Rust round-trip into native types: bitcode beats rkyv on log serialize (96.8 µs vs 178.9 µs), on minecraft_savedata serialize (82.0 µs vs 212.5 µs) and on log deserialize (1.145 ms vs 1.219 ms).

Very large archives on the default 32-bit relative pointers: one user hit an 'out of range integral type conversion' panic at about 1.2 GB (issue #657). The fix is the pointer_width_64 feature, which changes the wire format.

integration.dependencies: munge, ptr_meta, rancor, rend and rkyv_derive (a proc-macro using syn 3) are always pulled in. The default bytecheck feature adds bytecheck; the alloc feature adds hashbrown 0.17. Optional integrations cover arrayvec, bytes, hashbrown, indexmap, smallvec, smol_str, thin-vec, tinyvec, triomphe and uuid.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.81 (rust-version in Cargo.toml), edition 2021; CI tests stable, beta and nightly
integration.platforms: Any Rust target. CI tests x86_64 Linux, aarch64 macOS and x86_64 Windows, and cross-builds i686, i586, armv7, aarch64 Linux and thumbv6m-none-eabi. The hash-table SIMD path uses SSE2 on x86/x86_64 and NEON on little-endian aarch64, with a generic fallback everywhere else.
integration.thread_safety: No thread-safety guarantees are documented beyond Rust's type system. With std, the built-in scratch arena used by to_bytes is thread-local. Without std but with atomics, it is one global arena shared by all threads.

gotchas: The headline access and read figures (1.09 ns, 8.33 µs) come from unsafe access_unchecked, which skips all validation. Running it on untrusted bytes is undefined behavior; use access/from_bytes with the bytecheck feature for untrusted data.

Alignment and placement: the default format is aligned, so buffers need proper alignment (AlignedVec, or 16-byte alignment is usually enough). access also expects the root object to end exactly at the end of the buffer, so a length prefix or trailing bytes break it.

Endianness, alignment and pointer-width features change the wire format for the whole dependency graph. As a 0.x crate, archives are only compatible across semver-compatible releases (0.7 and 0.8 cannot read each other).

Safety history: RUSTSEC-2026-0233, -0234 and -0235 covered use-after-free and out-of-bounds reads that crafted archives triggered through the safe validated APIs; all three were patched in 0.8.17. Still open: #685 (a validated IndexMap/IndexSet can panic on lookup, a denial-of-service risk) and soundness reports #696/#697 about safe custom trait impls. rkyv_dyn (trait objects) is commented out of the workspace and pinned at 0.8.0-rc.1.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick rkyv when both ends are Rust and you want zero-copy access to ordinary Rust types (Vec, String, HashMap, BTreeMap, Rc) without maintaining an IDL. Pick YaFF or ProtoCache (C++ flat formats for Protobuf schemas) or the multi-language Apache Fory when C++ or another language must read the data, or when you need schema evolution.
verified_claims_summary: The source is rust_serialization_benchmark's CI run of 2026-09-10: rkyv 0.8.18 against the Rust crates capnp 0.27, flatbuffers 25.12.19, prost 0.14.4 and rmp-serde 1.3.1, built with rustc 1.100.0-nightly (LLVM 23.1.1), -C target-cpu=native and LTO, measured by Criterion on a 4-vCPU AMD EPYC 9V74 GitHub Actions VM. On the log dataset rkyv serialized in 178.87 µs, against 480.15 µs for capnp, 731.23 µs for prost, 763.63 µs for FlatBuffers and 1.318 ms for rmp-serde; it read unvalidated in 8.33 µs against 42.2 µs for FlatBuffers, and fully deserialized in 1.22 ms against 2.68 ms for prost decode. The baselines are Rust ports, not the C++ reference libraries, and the serialize loop reuses a pre-allocated 10 MB AlignedVec.
status_note: Actively maintained by its original author: 0.8.18 shipped on crates.io 2026-08-05, commits continue through 2026-09-25, and the crate has about 161M downloads. It is MIT-licensed and used as a normal Cargo dependency; require >=0.8.17 for untrusted input.
